items.stem: The primary purpose of paragraph 2 is to

options.text: establish that the campaign produced genuine help and genuine warmth, so that the critique to come cannot be dismissed as ingratitude
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 2 narrates concrete benefits (dialysis costs, gas, rent) and the affection in the donors' notes; the blueprint and paragraph 4's concession confirm the writer builds this warmth up before complicating it in paragraph 3 and 4.

options.text: show that the niece's persistence in building the page overcame Lenore's reluctance to have her face on the internet
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The niece winning the argument is one detail in the opening sentences; it does not account for the paragraph's catalog of what the money covered or the donors' notes.

options.text: suggest that former riders gave to the page largely out of guilt over debts they felt they still owed their driver
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The note 'you waited for me in the snow' expresses gratitude and affection; nothing in the paragraph frames the donations as guilt or repayment of a debt.

options.text: demonstrate that even a widely shared page fell short of covering the real costs of Lenore's illness and lost income
options.label: reversal
options.why: The paragraph says the page passed its goal in nine days and within a month covered the uncovered dialysis share, the gas, and three months of rent; it emphasizes success, not shortfall.

items.stem: The final sentence of the passage, "But she waited for every child, including the ones nobody else was watching for, and I can think of no better instruction for the rest of us," appeals to the audience primarily by

options.text: reassuring readers that Lenore herself would have endorsed the column's argument despite her dislike of public attention
options.label: reversal
options.why: The preceding sentence states plainly that Lenore would have disliked the column; the writer grounds the appeal in her documented behavior, not in her presumed approval.

options.text: turning the readers' admiration for Lenore into a reason to attend to unseen neighbors like Aurelio, so the demand feels like loyalty rather than rebuke
options.label: correct
options.why: The readers are donors who loved Lenore; 'the ones nobody else was watching for' recalls Aurelio from paragraph 3, and 'instruction for the rest of us' converts her habit of waiting for every child into a model for the community's conduct.

options.text: stirring readers' fear that their own children could one day be the ones left standing at the curb without anyone watching
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The sentence looks back to Lenore's conduct and forward to the readers' obligations toward the sick; it raises no threat to the readers' own children.

options.text: congratulating readers for having already followed Lenore's example when they gave to her page within nine days
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 6 asks readers to remember that the burden should never have fallen on them; the closing sentence issues an instruction still to be followed, not praise for a task completed.

items.stem:
The writer wants to replace sentence 12 (reproduced below) with wording that sounds sincere and purposeful rather than offhand, in a tone suited to a library's public blog.

Anyway, that is pretty much what the night is about.

Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: That, in the end, is the whole purpose of Transfer Night: making sure no earned credit goes to waste.
options.label: correct
options.why: Drops the dismissive 'anyway' and 'pretty much,' states the purpose plainly, and keeps a warm but serious public tone.

options.text: So yeah, that's basically the deal with Transfer Night, more or less, if you think about it.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Stays casual and hedging, which is the problem the writer wants to fix.

options.text: It is therefore incumbent upon all prospective matriculants to apprehend the night's essential function.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Stiff, bureaucratic diction that would put off library patrons unsure they belong.

options.text: Transfer Night guarantees that every reader will be admitted to a four-year university next fall.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Overpromises an outcome the post never supports.

items.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 4 and 5 into one sentence that keeps the contrast between Arturo leaving high school early and later finishing a degree. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Last year I met Arturo Pell, who had left high school at seventeen for his uncle's tire shop but at forty-one had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley.
options.label: correct
options.why: Joins the facts concisely and uses 'but' to keep the contrast between the early exit and the later achievement.

options.text: Last year I met Arturo Pell, who had left high school at seventeen, so at forty-one he had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: 'So' implies leaving school caused the degree, which is not a cause-effect link.

options.text: Last year I met Arturo Pell, he had left high school at seventeen for a tire shop, and at forty-one he had just finished a degree.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Comma splice after 'Pell'; also loses the contrast by using a plain 'and.'

options.text: Last year I met Arturo Pell, a forty-one-year-old who worked in a tire shop and was trying to sort out his nursing credits.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Concise, but it drops both the early school exit and the finished degree, so the contrast is gone.

items.stem: In sentence 3, the writer wants to punctuate the phrase giving the event's date so that it is set off correctly from the rest of the sentence. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors
options.label: correct
options.why: Commas enclose the nonessential phrase and correctly separate the weekday from the date.

options.text: Our annual Transfer Night held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors
options.label: convention_error
options.why: No opening comma, so the phrase is left half set off.

options.text: Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday April 17 brings advisors
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Leaves out the comma between weekday and date and the closing comma after the phrase.

options.text: Our annual Transfer Night; held this year on Thursday, April 17; brings advisors
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Semicolons have to join independent clauses; they cannot set off a modifying phrase.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 13 ("Hope to see you there.") with a closing line whose tone reassures adults who, as sentence 1 notes, are not sure they belong at the event. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Bring your questions and your old transcripts; there is a chair waiting for you, whatever your story.
options.label: correct
options.why: Warm, direct invitation that picks up the folding chairs from sentence 1 and tells uncertain readers they are welcome.

options.text: Only serious, well-prepared applicants should attend, since advisors have limited time for each visitor.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Discourages exactly the uncertain readers the writer wants to reassure.

options.text: Seriously, you totally have to come, it's going to be super fun and amazing for everyone!
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Gushing and slangy; it also contains a comma splice and does not deal with readers' doubts.

options.text: Parking is available behind the library, and the coffee urn will be refilled throughout the evening.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives logistics but does nothing to reassure readers that they belong.
